title: Planning ground based utility scale solar energy as green infrastructure to enhance ecosystem services
abstract: The agricultural sector is often characterized by monocultures and high company fragmentation that led to biodiversity loss and compromised important ecosystem functions, among these the pollination. Pollination is necessary for the health of ecological and agricultural systems, since they guarantee the fecundation of 80% of flower-flora species. This service is valuated among 235 and 577 billion dollars each year. Land use change is among the potential cause of pollinator's reduction. In most southern Italian regions, as Apulia, there was a land use competition between agriculture and renewable energy production, in particular photovoltaic (PV) system, due to the European policy aiming to decarbonize the energy production. Lot of agriculture companies moved toward the PV development to retrieve certain revenue, thanks to legislative and fiscal policies encouraging PV development. Here we propose a methodology to harmonize energy production, agriculture and the enhancement of ecosystem services, looking for a synergy between different economic activities and stakeholders. Areas occupied by PV system can be used for other purposes, as grazing or cultivation or educational activities. Naturalization activities can give back these spaces to pollinator populations notwithstanding the presence of PV panels, enhancing the pollination ecosystem service without affecting other agricultural areas.

## 1. Introduction

Ecosystems, if adequately managed and used by human, can support directly and indirectly a wide range of human services fundamental for social and economic support of present and future generation, called ecosystem services. However, the increasing and unsustainable anthropogenic pressures are depleting biodiversity and compromising the provision of ecosystem services. In the past decades biodiversity loss has been so dramatic that it has been recognized as crucial in the context of global change (Walker and Steffen, 1996) and quality of human life. Recently, society has increased its awareness that natural resources are becoming greatly compromised by the overexploitation of biodiversity, and the factors that limit socio-economic development are not technological, but natural (Daily, 1997; Petrosillo et al., 2010).

Pollination by animals is a keystone process in both human managed and natural terrestrial ecosystems underpinning biodiversity and ecosystem services. The importance of pollination as an ecosystem service is widely recognized (MEA, 2005; Potts et al., 2010a), because it

provides numerous benefits to society as food productions, farmers and beekeepers livelihoods and cultural values (Potts et al., 2016).

Animal pollination, guaranteeing the fertilisation of about 87% of flowering plant species (Ollerton et al., 2011), is indispensable for the health and function of both natural and agricultural systems, crop production and food security (Potts et al., 2010a; Ghazoul, 2005). Pollination is particularly important for agriculture productivity since more than 70% of the world crops depend on animal pollination and most of these crops are effectively pollinated by bees (Aizen et al., 2009; Klein et al., 2007), resulting the most important group of pollinators.

Many scholars have attempted to estimate the economic value of pollination (Hanley et al., 2015). Costanza et al. (1997) provided a global estimate at US$ 117·billion. More recently Gallai et al. (2009) have presented a methodologically improved estimation of the total economic value of pollination worldwide amounted to €153 billion, and specifically to €22 billion for Europe, highlighting that 10% of the total economic value of European food production is dependent upon insect

pollination.

The economic benefits provided by pollinators are not equally distributed worldwide. The greatest benefits are placed in southern and eastern Asia and Mediterranean Europe because of greater production of highly pollinator-dependent crops and higher market prices (Potts et al., 2016).

In recent decades, however, pollinators have been exposed to growing pressures from climate change, loss and fragmentation of (semi-)natural habitats, increasing use of pesticides, spread of pathogens and introduction of invasive alien species (Potts et al., 2016; Vanbergen et al., 2013). These factors resulted in severe wild and domestic pollinators decline in many regions worldwide (Biesmeijer et al., 2006; Ghazoul, 2005; Potts et al., 2010a) with ecological and economic consequences. Specifically, both managed and wild bee pollinators have undergone marked declines mainly in the US (NRC, 2006; vanEngelsdorp et al., 2008; Bartomeus et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2011) and some European countries (Biesmeijer et al., 2006; Bommarco et al., 2012; Potts et al., 2010b).

Given the importance of pollinators to crop production, food security, maintenance of wider biodiversity and ecosystem function and the evidence of their decline, several international and regional initiatives have been established to tackle the issues of pollinator declines and to monitor their status and promote their conservation. On a global scale, the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2000 has established the International initiative for the conservation and sustainable use of pollinators, also known as “IPI - International Pollinator Initiative” (http://www.cbd.int/decision/cop/?id=7147). But also at national and regional scales several programmes have promoted actions to protect the services provided by pollinators such as the Brazilian Pollinators Initiative (http://www.webbee.org.br/bpi/index.htm), the African Pollinators Initiative (http://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Pages/ Biosystematics/African-Pollinator-Initiative-(API).aspx), the European Pollinator Initiative (http://www.europeanpollinatorinitiative.org/), and the North American Pollinator Protection Campaign (http:// pollinator.org/nappc/), which includes Mexico, Canada and the USA.

## 1.1. The context of reference

the engine of Italian food production. The Apulia region (Fig. 1) tops the national table with 271,754 farms (16.8% of the total for Italy), 1,287,107.32 ha of farmland (10% of the national total) and a turnover of more than 2.3 billion euros in 2011.

The agricultural sector is often characterized by excessive recourse to monoculture and high fragmentation of farms, which have led to severe loss of biodiversity and associated ecosystemic functions such as pollination (Kremen et al., 2002; Winfree et al., 2009; Potts et al., 2010a).

Land-use change is one potential cause of the reduction in pollinator communities (Kremen et al. 2007), together with climate change, the use of pesticides and herbicides, fragmentation of habitats and invasion by alien species (Potts et al., 2016).

In addition, in southern Italy and in particular in Apulia region, a further problem that has emerged in the last few years is the full-scale competition for use of land between agriculture and renewable energy production, the result of specific European policies aimed to decarbonize the economy (Directive 2001/77/CE). For this reason, many crops have converted to photovoltaic electricity generation in return for certain earnings, helped by legislation (D.Lgs. 29/12/2003, n.387) and tax breaks (D.M. 19/02/2007) as well by intrinsic regional characteristics, such as topography and high solar irradiance: Apulia has more installed photovoltaic capacity than any other region in Italy and in 2015 it has detected the national record in terms of installed power with 2,600 (GSE, 2016).

This can be linked to two reasons: optimal environmental characteristics to guarantee high productivity of electrical energy from renewable sources and Regional laws that have favoured the installation of renewable energy production (L.R. n. 31 del 14.10.2008).

The generation of electricity through PV systems is acknowledged as a feasible solution against climate change that provides significant environmental benefits in comparison to the conventional (fossil) energy production (De Marco et al., 2014). The efforts toward a renewable energy system in low-economy areas and in developing nations, in substitution to conventional energy, are meant to reduce environmental impacts of fast growing populations and economies.

However, the realization of ground based photovoltaic systems requires suitable space and several environmental impacts on landscapes and biodiversity may result from site modifications, such as clearing of

vegetation, grading of land, redirecting water flow, fencing, creating access roads and pouring concrete pads to mount electrical equipment (Chiabrando et al., 2009; Fthenakis and Kim, 2009; Hernandez et al., 2014; Lakhani et al., 2014; Tsoutsos et al., 2005; Turney and Fthenakis, 2011). In the last decade, the number and size of the installations of large-scale photovoltaic arrays increased at a fast pace, for this reason the attention towards their impacts in terms of land-use and land transformation has been growing (Chiabrando et al., 2009), as well as concerns about landscape preservation and possible losses of ecosystem services (Scognamiglio, 2016) and biodiversity (Lovich and Ennen, 2011; Hernandez et al., 2014). Indirect effects on wildlife could result by the limitation of plant food resources, especially if pollinators are negatively affected (Lovich and Ennen, 2011).

It is recognized that humans have modified the provision of several ecosystem services by enhancing the delivery of a particular service (Foley et al., 1995; Rodriguez et al., 2006), causing trade-offs among ecosystem services (deVries et al., 2003). In the case of solar energy, although the installation of PV systems on landscape on a global scale seems to support the provision of the ecosystem service “climate regulation” by avoiding the emissions of GHG, there is a growing recognition that it may have substantial impacts on a range of local proximal ecosystem services (Omer, 2009) (i.e. pollination, recreation).

However, several studies suggested that the installation of the renewable energy system could increase the biodiversity in used areas (Peschel, 2010). There are significant opportunities to actively manage solar farms for enhancing biodiversity, i.e. extensive grassland and/or wildflower meadows between and/or beneath solar panels and in field margins, bird boxes and ponds (BirdLife Europe, 2011; BRE, 2014). Recently, a study on 11 solar farms across the UK (Montag et al., 2016) has investigated whether solar farms can promote biodiversity, with benefits to wildlife and potentially even surrounding crops. Specifically, researchers have compared solar farms to adjacent equivalent undeveloped sites on the same farms that were under similar management practices prior to solar installation. The results were a significant increase in bird diversity, broadleaf plant diversity, wildflowers and many other species such as butterflies and bumblebees. Of course, the level of benefit to biodiversity was highly dependent on the management of the site (solar farms periodically grazed or seeded with wildflowers). Solar farms could be ideal environments for bee habitats because they can support a range of attractive micro-habitats (BRE, 2014). In this perspective, Solarcentury and Bumblebee Conservation Trust (BBCT) have partnered to promote the development of bee-friendly environments by creating biodiverse spaces in and around the solar farms.

Moreover other publications focus on the integration of solar farms with the landscape (Chiabrando et al., 2009; Kapetanakis et al., 2014). In addition Scognamiglio (2016) has advanced the idea that a new approach in designing and assessing large scale PV systems may help to reduce environmental impacts and offer new possibilities for ecosystem services. Particularly important is the “pore” space, that is “the space around” or “the space in between” the modules. There are many uses of the “pore space”, for example grazing (Denholm and Margolis, 2008), harvesting, biodiversity, biking, that increase the provision of ecosystem services delivered by the solar farm.

In this perspective, we have developed a project idea that proposes to evolve the photovoltaic energy plants in southern Italy, especially in Apulia region, into “new urban photo-ecological gardens”. The idea was carried out with the aim to design and plan a multifunctional use of solar farms allowing to improve their ecological performances, exploit local biodiversity with habitats and vegetation of high conservation value and to support a broader portfolio of ecosystem services.

The areas set aside for photovoltaic solar farms can be used for measures that favour the growth of pollinator insects, thereby avoiding the use of agricultural land. Some regional authorization procedures for solar farms impose a ban on pesticides in fields occupied by photovoltaic panels; this makes the fields suitable for crops with a very low

environmental impact. By favouring the growth of bees and butterflies, they can become net producers of pollinators, generating benefits for the surrounding area.

The aim is to harmonize energy production, agriculture and the safeguard of ecological processes that underpin human well-being, creating a strong synergism between economic and institutional players in the regions of southern Italy.

## 2. Methodology: the multidisciplinary nature of the proposal

The idea arose from collaboration between Globar Solar Fund Group (GSF), an industrial firm founded in 2008, which operates in the photovoltaic energy sector, and professionals in the landscape ecology and environmental impact assessment sectors. GSF is the main producer of photovoltaic energy in Apulia, managing 174 solar farms with an installed capacity of 138 MW and an annual average production of 222 GWh, avoiding the emission of 112,000 t of CO2.

In particular, GSF desired to develop a regional brand that could combine renewable energy generation with the improvement of the ecological functions of landscape in which the company operates, while the experts to propose a project in the agricultural field that could support the well-being of the region and the people who live there.

As simple and linear as the idea is (Fig. 2), it adopts a multidisciplinary approach in order to develop a management system for the areas in, between and around the photovoltaic panels that enables economic, ecological and social aspects to coexist without causing trade-off among them.

The first step was a multi-scale study of the context of reference and the main ecological issues, especially pollination and honey production, which have implications on both the local scale, i.e. their compatibility with the application of the project, and the global scale, going way beyond the municipality in which the measures are planned.

The Apulia region shows a spatial pattern mainly characterized by arable lands destined to cereals production and intensive olive groves (www.sit.puglia.it/). These areas are characterized by a low relative pollination potential (Zulian et al., 2013). In olive groves, the mowing of undergrowth vegetation further reduces the biodiversity in such areas (Fig. 3).

In the last years, the wide dissemination of solar farms changed the landscape structure in Apulia region by creating holes in the spatial pattern (perforation) (Forman 1995, Turner et al., 2001). The idea is to use this process of landscape transformation to support pollination by implementing current solar farms in sinks and sources for biodiversity (Fig. 4).

The second step was aimed to characterize, with the support of GSF, the photovoltaic solar farms in terms of:

□ construction type, i.e. characterization of the main types of solar

   - farms: used technologies, height of the panels from the ground, distance between panels, free spaces from panels and maximum temperatures recorded within the solar farm;

- soil and vegetation types: mainly the solar farms were agricultural land; therefore we characterized the current vegetation to assess whether the present plants can support pollination or other ecological processes;

- type of maintenance required for the panels and vegetation: characterization of the activities carried out by GSF to reduce the risk of fire, shading of the panels and false alarms of the security system created by uncontrolled vegetation growth;

- company requirements: GSF wants to combine energy production with environmental protection;

- costs: identification of the costs supported by GSF for the maintenance of solar farms, both as quantified costs of specific maintenance work as well as qualitative evaluation of other specific activities (check for false alarms, evaluation of efficiency loss for the shading etc.).

On the basis of this characterization, the next step was to provide a concrete vision of how these ecosystem services could be delivered within the photovoltaic solar farms belonging to GSF. It was then necessary to consult an expert in botany to determine which plants were most suited to being cultivated on the solar farms, given the aim of favouring endemic melliferous vegetation while promoting conservation and economically viable production. In addition, it was decided that this vegetation should include plants of medicinal value, in order to obtain an additional economic asset. Once a spectrum of suitable species and possible habitats had been identified, a commercial plant nursery was consulted in order to analyse the issue in terms of economic

feasibility, also taking account of the risk of Xylella Fastidiosa infection, present in Apulia throughout the Salento peninsula (sub-region of southern Apulia which includes the entire province of Lecce, almost all of Brindisi and part of the province of Taranto).

To reinforce the regional branding, a professional graphic designer was involved to represent the project in a simple and direct way, in order to broaden the range of potential targets as much as possible without discriminating in terms of social and cultural background (Supplementary Fig. 1). The role of the graphic artist also proved to be fundamental for the project designers: working with an expert from a different field helped to highlight the project's potential flaws and provided important feedback that helped to clarify and improve the more technical aspects that the public are less aware of.

Finally, considering that many solar farms are sited near urban areas, there is also a proposal to improve the social impacts of the projects developing educational activities linked to the environmental aspects, use of sustainable energy and biodiversity arising from the project. In this way the community can have a positive attitude toward “new urban photo-ecological gardens” because the social acceptance of a new infrastructure is possible when the welfare decreasing-aspects of the project are balanced by welfare- increasing aspects such as economic development, energy supply security, green benefits, community compensation (Cohen et al., 2014; Devine-Wright, 2011). With reference to this project, a quantitative evaluation of social impact from “new urban photo-ecological gardens” has not been considered, since it depends on multiple factors and characteristics of the plant (location, accessibility to the site, similar educational activities on-going in the community) and will be addressed in the implementation of the project in each plant.

Thanks to its multidisciplinary approach, this project goes beyond a vision of planning that sees planning of biodiversity and planning of ecosystem services as irreconcilable, developing an idea that goes in both directions.

## 3. Results and discussion: the proposed new urban photoecological gardens

It is widely accepted that technology has a crucial role to play in tackling the issues that humanity is now faced with, and it is this principle that inspired the project we call “Photovoltaic Parks: New ” Photo-Ecological Urban Gardens .

The innovative element of the project lies in the proposal to exploit the fertile areas used for solar energy production, replacing the current flora with valuable plants. The central idea of the project described here is to apply this type of integration, already proposed in northern Europe for the construction of new solar energy farms, in an innovative way to existing photovoltaic power plants in Apulia.

The presentation of the idea was preceded by preliminary activities conducted on solar farms owned by GSF.

Fig. 4. Representative diagram of the spatial pattern that characterizes the Apulia region before and after the introduction of solar farms in the landscape.

Fig. 5. Main vegetation found in the inspected solar farms.

The solar panels analysed are surrounded by invasive herbaceous vegetation with no valuable floral elements. The flora was chatacterized by ruderal, nitrophilous species, requiring frequent cutting curtail (at a cost of about € 3,300/MWp per each mowing) to reduce the risk of fires and prevent them from casting shade on the panels. The company applies around two mowing plants per year for each solar farm.

Specifically, the main plant species found were: Avena barbata L. (Poaceae); Inula viscosa L. (Asteraceae); Reichardia picroides (L.), Conyza albida Spreng; Calendula arvensis L (Vaill.); Cichorium intybus (L); Echium vulgare L; Chrysanthemum oronarium L.; Conyza canadensis Cronq. (Asteraceae); Opopanax chironius L; Malva sylvestris L. (Malvaceae); Reichardia picroides Roth. (Asteraceae); Sonchus oleraceus L. (Asteraceae); Sorghum halepense L. and Veronica arvensis L. (Fig. 5).

By replacing the present vegetation with autochthonous melliferous and medicinal flora, “photo-ecological gardens” will be multifunctional patches characterized by heterogeneous habitats able to attract several insects and, for this reason, they could be set up where bee-keepers can bring their bees to forage. It is recognized that different habitats, such as forest edges, grasslands rich in flowers, offer suitable sites for wild pollinator insects such as solitary or honey bees, bumblebees or butterflies (Kells and Goulson, 2003; Svensson et al., 2000; Westphal et al., 2003). As soon as these insects start foraging, ecosystems that host these insect populations have the potential to increase the yield of adjacent crops that are dependent on insect mediated pollination (Carvalheiro et al., 2011). Solar tracking technologies, such as the double-axis tracker developed by GSF, are more suited to this project because they avoid cones of permanent shade on the soil.

Data provided by GSF for their 1 MW double-axis tracker plants show that the maximum temperature recorded on the ground inside the solar farms is similar to the atmospheric temperature (according to the temperature recorded by the weather station localized in the solar farms and by the sensors located on each panel).

This observation differs with respect to other studies (Fthenakis and Yu, 2013) reporting the development of high temperatures in large

solar farms such as those localized in North America and in other parts of the world, due to PV panels converting most of the incident solar radiation into heat. This can alter the air-flow and temperature profiles near the panels and can affect the thermal environment of near-by populations of humans and other species.

The lack of similar temperature increase in analysed PV farms can be related to the small size of the plant (< 1 MW) and the adopted tracker technology, in which panels are about 1.5 m from the ground level and rotate, allowing a greater aeration below the panel. The time of flower blooms (from February to May and from September to November) does not coincide with the period in which Apulia recorded the maximum temperatures (from July to August). Therefore, a temperature problem should not occur during the honey production period. In addition plants able to thrive in terrain exposed to strong solar irradiation, prolonged drought and sharp variations in temperature will be preferred, using indigenous germplasm adapted to the ecological context of the area.

It has to be noticed that, according to the official statistic on solar farms in the Apulia Region (GSE, 2017), 16% of solar farms have a power up to 200 kW, 62% up to 1 MW e 21% with a power greater than 1 MW.

The study considered two types of space available within the photovoltaic solar farms:

□ Type 1: free areas, belonging to the farms but not occupied by panels, generally along the edges of the property; □ Type 2: the areas where the panels are installed.

The plants and floral associations will be chosen on the basis of their phytogeographical value, melliferous capacity and potential use in the phytotherapy industry. The choice will also depend on whether the solar farms are sited near agricultural processing companies, the experience of local personnel and whether the crops are characteristic of the area. Obviously any restrictions arising from norms designed to

contain Xylella fastidiosa in areas where it has been detected must be taken into account.

The Type 1 areas will contain maquis and garrigue vegetation, with rosemary, oregano, savory and thyme. These are melliferous formations rich in aromatic and medicinal species with potential applications in phytotherapy and cosmetics. Of particular phytogeographical value is the garrigue vegetation with microphylls such as Erica forskali and Anthyllis hermanniae, two plants of particular value listed as being at risk of extinction. “Apulia heather” (Erica forskalii = Erica manipuliflora) is a shrub described as “vulnerable” (in accordance with the IUCN categories) in the Red List of species at risk of extinction in Italy. Anthyllis hermanniae, together with its sub-species japigica, is a very rare species cited in the Apulia Regional Red List, mainly endemic along the coast of Salento.

Small stands of trees can be planted in the free areas on the north side of the solar farms, so as not to throw shadow on the panels. These stands of trees would mitigate the impact on the landscape and would play a key role in terms of conservation, since they could be used to reconstitute various priority natural habitat types and natural habitat types of Community interest (Directive 92/43/EC), including “Quercus ilex and Quercus rotundifolia forests” (habitat code 9340) and “Olea and Ceratonia forests” (habitat code 9320).

This would have the dual advantage of increasing biodiversity and enabling flowering at various times during the year, ensuring longer periods for bee-keeping applications.

Regarding woods of Quercus (L., 1753), the idea is to reforest the free areas of the solar farms with small stands of oaks in order to recreate suitable conditions not only for honey making but also for the growth of truffles by inoculating the plants’ roots with mycorrhiza.

In Salento, in reforested areas, two wild species of truffle can be found: Tuber aestivum (the Burgundy Truffle, locally called Scorzone) and the more valuable Tuber albidum (the White Truffle, locally called Bianchetto). They were first recorded in Salento a few decades ago and can be harvested late, when the truffle season has finished in those regions of Italy that have traditionally been famous for this delicacy. This is attracting funs of truffle harvesting in Salento, generating a new type of tourism.

The Type 2 areas can be used for cultivating Fabaceae species such as red clover and white clover. These perennial herbaceous melliferous plants do not exceed 30 cm in height and can thus be cultivated between the panels without compromising their efficiency or the maintenance of the individual units. As an alternative to clover, Medicago sativa could also be cultivated. This plant is also short (not exceeding 80 cm). Both plants have extensive therapeutic applications.

A new approach is thus required, shifting from “negative vegetation management” (Fig. 6), aimed mainly at the elimination of invasive plants, to “active vegetation management”, i.e. the cultivation of plants with an economic and ecological value. The identified plants do not require specific professional skills and regular gardeners can thus be employed, making use of local botanical gardens in the start-up phase.

For spaces of about 1,000m[2] , the costs of purchasing and planting are estimated at about € 3,000 for woodland to about € 4,500 for garrigue, while for the meadows (which may require a second sowing) the price would fall to about € 500.

All the plants will grow autonomously, with no need for annual maintenance to ensure growth. For the arboreal and shrub plants, irrigation will initially be necessary in order to get through the hottest periods, with a maximum of six operations during the first two years in the period May-September, supplying about 20 l/plant (about € 600 for the entire period per 1,000m[2] ).

The average size of 1 MW solar farms is 25,000-30,000m[2] ; therefore, the costs of vegetation introduction ranges from € 10,000 to € 28,000 per MW on first three years of project life, depending on the type (woodland, garrigue and meadows) and the amount of vegetation to be introduced.

The choice of melliferous plants aims to honey production: it can be

foreseen a honey production varying from 300 kg to 450 kg for MW (Amicabile, 2015). Considering an average market price of about 18 € per kg (2017 price on detail selling price), the estimated revenue ranges between €5,400 and €8,100 per MW/year. Additional honey-related products like Royal jelly, honeydew, have also a market appeal. Moreover, other economic activities related to such crops can be considered, like medicinal production.

The ban on pesticides enacted on most of PV fields, allows the selling of aforementioned products potentially as organic, available on the market at a higher price than conventional agriculture products.

The advantages for the PV companies are multiple. Besides the economic return on such cultivation, which are dependent on the management, the most important advantages are summarized as follows:

- avoid of mowing costs;

- reduction of the risk for fire;

- reduction of false alarm for the security laser fence.

Some of these costs can be quantified in detail, such as the mowing activities, others lack of specific quantification but represent a management cost for the Company. Just considering the mowing cost, it amounts to €18,000 in three years, returning the investment for the average vegetation introduction costs as described.

There are also other advantages whose economic quantification is almost not predictable at the moment: such benefits mostly relate to the corporate image for the Company, in the field of environmental protection, because agricultural patches subtracted from agriculture can be returned as agro-ecosystems, and the enhancement of ecosystem services in favour of near farmers.

## 3.1. Possible targets

This project acts as a Territorial Brand Action to create a definite vision of GSF: a company working "for" and "with" the territory. This would create a harmony between energy production and territorial sustainability through actions that create positive feedback between business management of solar farms and development of ecosystem services in the territory.

For GSF a key point ensuring the feasibility of the project is the reduction in maintenance costs due to the fact that the plants would not require frequent mowing. The technical and economic commitments arising from the management of the crops could be contracted to third parties, who would use them to produce honey and medicinal plants, generating added value for local businesses.

There are many potential targets that would benefit from this innovative solution. Indeed, the idea for the project can be developed in all solar farms in southern Italy with specific reference to Apulia region, the main player in Italian solar energy production. The main target companies are thus producers of renewable energy, together with other local economic players, like bee-keepers and companies that produce medicinal goods.

Therefore, the whole society would benefit from it because pollination is a fundamental ecosystem service for food security (Potts et al., 2010a) (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Solar farms managed in this way could have a natural fit with regional entities (schools, educational farms, research bodies) and would enhance the teaching seminars on biodiversity. In addition, the weather station used for the acquisition of meteorological data used to evaluate PV panels performance would provide valuable support to research bodies, making it possible to study the correlation between biocenosis, the production of honey and climate change. Considering that bees are highly sensitive to sources of pollution, a further benefit would be a natural regional monitoring network, useful for studying the state of the environment. The photovoltaic energy plants would thus evolve into “new urban photo-ecological gardens”. In Fig. 7 a conceptual design

scheme has been extrapolated analysing the pattern of solar farms managed by GSF. Therefore, this model represents the main type of systems found in the territory under study:

- ➢ Perimeter and roads to facilitate the circulation of vehicles;

This represents the reference model for the project and this scheme will be explained during the final and executive project considering the characteristics of each solar farm. The definitive design will probably require the support of other professionals as landscape architects to better optimize the planning of these interventions and agronomist to better study the techniques of planting the vegetation.

Of course, the design idea we developed was focused on existing solar farms and for this reason we could not act on the spatial patterns of the panels, so we had to choose the vegetation also depending on the type of solar farms. In new photovoltaic plants, the introduction of honeyed vegetation could be planned together with the arrangement of the panels, also referring to the research of Scognamiglio (2016) that, with a critical review, proposed the idea that PV systems should be designed as an element of the landscape they belong to, according to an 'inclusive' design approach that focuses on the overall energy efficiency of the system and other additional ecological and landscape objectives.

This “new urban photo-ecological gardens” in the peri-urban and agricultural landscape could represent a source of biodiversity and ecosystem services because improves the presence of vegetation with important ecological role in the monocultural landscape. In this way, “new urban photo-ecological gardens” can constitute the stepping-stones for the specie the move in the landscape. Indeed the large presence of this green infrastructures in mono-cultural landscape could support the network of nature at both local: for bees and other local insects and animals that can use these plants as a habitat; broad scale: for species of migratory birds that can find refuge in these new habitats (Fig. 8).

In peri-urban area new urban photo-ecological gardens could replace the function of natural areas and so have important role in mental health. There is in fact evidence for a positive relationship between access to natural environments and people's perceived overall general health, mental health, physical health and social health (Thompson et al., 2012; Wolch et al., 2014). The contact with natural environments promotes psychological restoration, improved mood and attention and reduces stress and anxiety. It could have positive effect to cognitive restoration, self-discipline, reduced aggression and reduce crime (Thompson et al., 2012).

So, this project shows how it is possible to promote ecosystem services and biodiversity in the same time and place without trade-off. This approach is fundamental to overpass the concept that planning for biodiversity and ecosystem services conservation at the same time and in the same place may be difficult because areas important for

Indeed, even though the persistence of biodiversity and the maintenance of ecosystem services are largely dependent upon each other, actually, these two aspects are not wholly interchangeable (Williams and Araújo, 2002).

The land occupied by solar farms, do not represent anymore land taken away from agricultural production, but multifunctional land for economic activities: production of electricity, production of honey and medicinal plants; ecological role: enhancement of ecosystem services related to pollination and social role: ensure the welfare of the population by supporting food production and social activity.

## 4. Conclusions and policy implications

Biodiversity loss and the degradation of ecosystems and the services they provide are major concerns facing modern society.

The valorization of biodiversity and ecosystem services requires not only the detailed study of ecosystem distribution and functioning, but also the adoption of tailored political strategies, such as those proposed by the EU in its Biodiversity 2020 Strategy (UE, 2011). As pointed out in this strategy for biodiversity protection, the development of green infrastructures can have an important role for the restoration of degraded ecosystems and protects our natural capital. The European Commission defines green infrastructure as “a strategically planned network of natural, semi-natural and artificial networks areas with other environmental features designed and managed to deliver a wide range of ecosystem services” (CE, 2013). They include green and blue spaces, as parks and reserves, sporting fields, riparian areas like stream and river banks, greenways and trails, community gardens, street trees, and nature conservation areas, as well as less conventional spaces such as green walls, green alleyways, and cemeteries (Roy et al., 2012). They are present in rural and urban settings. The definition stresses three

important aspects: a network of areas, regional planning and management and the concept of ecosystem services, which implies the concepts of ecological connectivity and conservation as well as the multifunctional character of ecosystems (Mubareka et al., 2013).

The concept of green infrastructure emphasises the quality as well as quantity of urban, peri-urban green spaces and natural areas (Turner, 1996; Rudlin and Falk, 1999), their multifunctional role (Sandstr ̈om, 2002), and the importance of interconnections between habitats (Vander Ryn and Cowan, 1996). If a green infrastructure is proactively planned, developed, and maintained it has the potential to guide urban development by providing a framework for economic growth and nature conservation (Walmsley, 2006; Schrijnen, 2000; Vander Ryn and Cowan, 1996).

In this perspective, our project shows that solar plants, if properly localized, designed and managed over time, can represent a green infrastructure providing wildlife habitats, encouraging the presence of species of high conservation value and strengthening the ecological network with environmental, economic, educational and recreational benefits at multiple scales.

In line with the multifunctional character of landscape, a proper planning, design and management of a solar farm should require a multidisciplinary approach: the design skills of engineering must be integrated with sustainable and environmental sciences related to landscape and urban planning. This is in line with the multifunctional character of landscape; conservation policy and management should be interdisciplinary. They should build on solid knowledge of ecological, social and economic processes and define opportunities and priorities with a view to achieve both the conservation objectives of the sites and sustainable socio-economic development (Semeraro et al., 2015).

Moreover, they should also think about how these systems may evolve over time even if the plant was no longer used for this purpose.

Solar farms have a useful life of about 20/30 years, depending mostly on the yield of the panels. At the end of their useful life, the

panels need to be dismantled and the brown fields to be recovered. In the absence of new projects by managers that decommission solar farms, the land would then cease to be managed, becoming invaded by weeds of little ecological or economic value.

However, the company could also decide to prolong the life of the solar farm by replacing the old panels with new ones. As technology improves, increasingly efficient panels will be produced. Thus, for the same land area the installed capacity will be greater. The capacity of the old units can be increased simply by replacing the panels with higherspecification new ones, without increasing the land area used or the number of panels installed.

This policy could however result in problems of a procedural and administrative nature, with reference to present Italian legislation, since the initial concession agreements specify limits to the amount of power generated. The natural solution to these legal restrictions would be to reduce the area of land covered by the new panels, although this would clearly be uneconomic for the company, as well as counterproductive, given the growing demand for electricity in a country such as Italy, especially in the light of the commitment to reduce the use of fossil fuels under the EU's Horizon 2020 policy.

The transformation of photovoltaic solar farms into “new urban photo-ecological gardens” could provide an occasion and an incentive for the gradual conversion of old power plants into new ones, installing state-of-the-art equipment with greater power-generating capacity per unit area, resulting in lesser impact on the landscape and environment.

The simple installation of new, more efficient panels would not entail substantial new impacts on the areas of interest, while the measures to boost biodiversity and increase ecosystem services would enhance the ecological, social and economic value of the areas. Analysing the distribution of the photovoltaic energy farms and the regional context in which the project is being implemented, this would also support the regional ecological network, with positive effects even beyond regional boundaries. Obviously this would require modifications to the national legal framework regulating the installation of photovoltaic solar farms.

Even in the case of definitive decommissioning of the solar power plant at the end of its useful life, the “new urban photo-ecological gardens” would prevent the complete abandonment of the area, allowing it to return to an uncultivated state, overgrown with invasive vegetation. Indeed, over time the vegetation introduced would become structural and would ensure continuity of the economic and ecological functions that developed beside the panels. Thus the area of the solar farm would not lose its role as a reserve and source of biodiversity.

These typology of projects, which represent green infrastructures to implement ecosystem services related to human activities, should be an integral part of the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA: Directive 2001/42/CE) and Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA: Directive 37/85/CEE) are tools aimed to evaluate environmental impacts on plan and projects, aimed to promote the sustainable development of human activities. An important part in any SEA and EIA is represented by the mitigation measures, actions to be implemented in order to mitigate the expected adverse environmental impacts. With regard to the renewable energy sector, the introduction of “new urban photo-ecological gardens” represent a mitigation measure that administrators (local, regional and national) should request in order to create added ecological and socio-economic value in the landscape. At Regional Level, such measures as well as those presented by other authors (Scognamiglio, 2016) could be introduced as mitigation measure in the Regional Environmental Energy Plan (Piano Energetico Ambientale Regionale: PEAR) that contains strategic guidelines and objectives in the energy field.
